subject: Aerodynamics and Stalls
learning_objective: Understand the relationship between angle of attack, airspeed, load factor, configuration, and stalls.
question_text: An airplane can be stalled at which combination of airspeed and flight attitude?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only at low airspeed and a high nose attitude

choices.label: B
choices.text: At any airspeed and in any attitude if the critical angle of attack is exceeded

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only below the published power-off stall speed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only when the engine is producing idle power

explanation: A stall occurs when the wing exceeds its critical angle of attack. This can happen at any airspeed, attitude, or power setting because stall speed changes with load factor, configuration, and other conditions.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A low airspeed and high nose attitude are common stall conditions, but they are not required.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Published stall speed applies only to specified test conditions; an accelerated stall can occur at a higher airspeed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A wing may stall with power on or power off.

handbook_reference: FAA-H-8083-25C, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5; FAA-S-ACS-6C PA.VII.B.K1

subject: Performance and Limitations
learning_objective: Apply aerodynamic principles affecting airplane performance.
question_text: In a coordinated level turn at 60 degrees of bank, approximately what load factor is imposed on the airplane?
explanation: For a coordinated level turn, load factor equals 1 divided by the cosine of the bank angle. The cosine of 60 degrees is 0.5, so the load factor is 2 G.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: About 1.4 G corresponds to a 45-degree level turn.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This is below the calculated load factor at 60 degrees.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A 60-degree coordinated level turn produces 2 G, not 3 G.

subject: Performance and Limitations
learning_objective: Understand how atmospheric conditions affect airplane performance.
question_text: What is the usual effect of high density altitude on a normally aspirated airplane?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shorter takeoff roll and increased climb performance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Longer takeoff roll and reduced climb performance

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower true airspeed for a given indicated airspeed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased engine power and propeller efficiency

explanation: High density altitude means the air behaves as though the airplane were operating at a higher altitude. Lower air density reduces engine power, propeller thrust, and wing performance, generally increasing takeoff distance and reducing rate of climb.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This describes the effect of lower density altitude.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: True airspeed for a given indicated airspeed generally increases as density altitude increases.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A normally aspirated engine and propeller generally produce less power and thrust in less-dense air.

subject: Weight and Balance
learning_objective: Understand how center-of-gravity location affects airplane performance and handling.
question_text: Compared with a forward center of gravity, an aft center of gravity within limits generally produces which effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Greater longitudinal stability and higher control forces

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reduced longitudinal stability and more difficult stall recovery

choices.label: C
choices.text: A higher stall speed in every configuration

choices.label: D
choices.text: No change in stability or stall recovery

explanation: Moving the center of gravity aft reduces the stabilizing tail-down force and decreases longitudinal stability. Stall and spin recovery can become more difficult because less nose-down pitching authority may be available.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A forward center of gravity generally provides greater longitudinal stability and requires greater control force.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An aft center of gravity does not necessarily produce a higher stall speed; it commonly reduces the indicated stall speed slightly, while reducing stability.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Center-of-gravity location materially affects stability, controllability, and recovery characteristics.

subject: Aircraft Systems
learning_objective: Understand pitot-static systems and associated flight instruments.
question_text: If the pitot opening becomes blocked but the drain hole remains open, what will the airspeed indicator normally indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zero

choices.label: B
choices.text: Airspeed that increases with altitude

choices.label: C
choices.text: Airspeed that decreases with altitude

choices.label: D
choices.text: The last indicated airspeed before the blockage

explanation: With the pitot opening blocked and the drain hole open, pitot pressure vents to the atmosphere. The airspeed indicator then receives essentially static pressure on both sides and normally indicates zero.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This behavior can occur when both the pitot opening and drain hole are blocked, trapping pitot pressure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This can also be associated with trapped pitot pressure during an altitude change, not an open drain.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The last airspeed is not retained when pitot pressure can escape through the open drain.

subject: Aircraft Systems
learning_objective: Understand static-system failures and their effect on flight instruments.
question_text: If the static port becomes completely blocked and no alternate static source is selected, how will the altimeter normally respond during a climb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It will continue to indicate the altitude at which the blockage occurred

choices.label: B
choices.text: It will indicate a rapid descent

choices.label: C
choices.text: It will read increasingly higher than actual altitude

choices.label: D
choices.text: It will unwind to zero feet

explanation: A completely blocked static port traps the existing static pressure in the altimeter case. Without changing static pressure, the altimeter remains at approximately the altitude where the blockage occurred.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A blocked static port does not normally command a descent indication.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The altimeter cannot sense decreasing outside pressure during the climb, so it does not continue increasing normally.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The instrument does not automatically return to zero when the static source is blocked.

subject: Weather Theory
learning_objective: Recognize characteristics associated with atmospheric stability.
question_text: Which combination is most commonly associated with stable air?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cumuliform clouds, turbulence, and good surface visibility

choices.label: B
choices.text: Stratiform clouds, smooth air, and possible poor visibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: Strong vertical currents and showery precipitation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dust devils and rapidly building cumulonimbus clouds

explanation: Stable air resists vertical motion. It commonly produces smooth flying conditions, stratiform clouds, steady precipitation, and reduced visibility in haze, smoke, or fog.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Cumuliform clouds and turbulence are more characteristic of unstable air.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Strong vertical currents and showery precipitation indicate instability.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Dust devils and rapidly growing cumulonimbus clouds are signs of unstable air.

subject: Weather Hazards
learning_objective: Understand thunderstorm development and associated hazards.
question_text: What event marks the beginning of the mature stage of a thunderstorm cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first appearance of a cumulus cloud

choices.label: B
choices.text: Precipitation beginning to fall from the cloud

choices.label: C
choices.text: The complete disappearance of updrafts

choices.label: D
choices.text: The anvil becoming detached from the cell

explanation: The mature stage begins when precipitation starts falling from the cloud. During this stage, updrafts and downdrafts coexist and the thunderstorm is generally at its greatest intensity.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A growing cumulus cloud is associated with the cumulus stage.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: When downdrafts dominate and updrafts disappear, the cell is entering the dissipating stage.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: An anvil may form during development, but its detachment does not define the mature stage.

subject: Weather Theory
learning_objective: Evaluate conditions favorable for fog or low-cloud formation.
question_text: If air temperature and dew point are converging while the wind is light, what weather development becomes increasingly likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fog or low clouds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clear air with rapidly improving visibility

choices.label: C
choices.text: Severe turbulence caused solely by the dew-point spread

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rapid increase in density altitude caused by dry air

explanation: A narrowing temperature-dew-point spread indicates the air is approaching saturation. With light wind and suitable cooling or moisture, fog or low cloud formation becomes increasingly likely.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Approaching saturation usually increases, rather than decreases, the risk of restricted visibility.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A small dew-point spread alone does not produce severe turbulence.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The condition indicates increasing relative humidity, not dry air.

subject: Human Factors
learning_objective: Recognize hypoxia and apply appropriate corrective action.
question_text: A pilot at altitude develops impaired judgment, headache, and unusual euphoria consistent with hypoxia. What is the most appropriate immediate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Use supplemental oxygen if available and descend to a lower altitude

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increase physical activity to improve circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Breathe more rapidly without changing altitude

choices.label: D
choices.text: Continue the flight because hypoxia symptoms normally resolve without action

explanation: Suspected hypoxia requires prompt correction. The pilot should use supplemental oxygen if available and descend to an altitude where adequate oxygenation can be maintained.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Physical exertion increases oxygen demand and may worsen hypoxia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Rapid breathing may cause hyperventilation and does not correct insufficient available oxygen.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Hypoxia can impair judgment and become life-threatening; continued exposure is unsafe.

subject: Human Factors
learning_objective: Recognize hyperventilation and apply corrective action.
question_text: What is an appropriate corrective action when a pilot recognizes symptoms of hyperventilation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consciously slow the breathing rate and breathe normally

choices.label: B
choices.text: Take rapid, deep breaths to increase oxygen intake

choices.label: C
choices.text: Climb immediately to a higher altitude

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hold the breath until all symptoms disappear

explanation: Hyperventilation removes carbon dioxide from the blood too quickly. Consciously slowing the breathing rate and restoring normal breathing helps correct the imbalance. If there is doubt whether symptoms are hypoxia or hyperventilation, supplemental oxygen should also be used if available.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Rapid, deep breathing is the cause of hyperventilation and can worsen symptoms.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Climbing reduces available oxygen and may introduce or worsen hypoxia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Prolonged breath-holding is not the recommended corrective technique.

subject: Federal Aviation Regulations
learning_objective: Calculate VFR fuel requirements, including required reserve.
question_text: Under 14 CFR 91.151, what is the minimum fuel reserve required for a daytime VFR flight in an airplane, assuming normal cruising speed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enough to fly for 20 minutes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enough to fly for 30 minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enough to fly for 45 minutes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enough to fly for 60 minutes

explanation: For daytime VFR flight in an airplane, the planned fuel supply must allow flight to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, at least 30 minutes beyond that point.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Twenty minutes does not meet the airplane daytime VFR reserve requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Forty-five minutes is the airplane nighttime VFR reserve requirement.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Part 91 does not prescribe a 60-minute reserve for this scenario.

subject: Federal Aviation Regulations
learning_objective: Apply regulations concerning alcohol and drug use by crewmembers.
question_text: Under 14 CFR 91.17, which statement describes a condition that prohibits a person from acting or attempting to act as a required flight crewmember?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alcohol was consumed within the preceding 8 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alcohol was consumed within the preceding 4 hours, provided blood alcohol is below 0.04 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alcohol was consumed the previous evening, regardless of elapsed time or impairment

choices.label: D
choices.text: The person has any detectable alcohol in the body, even when more than 8 hours have elapsed and there is no impairment

explanation: Section 91.17 prohibits acting or attempting to act as a required flight crewmember within 8 hours after consuming alcohol. It also separately prohibits acting while under the influence, while using a drug that affects faculties contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or greater.

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The regulation specifies 8 hours, not 4 hours, and the restrictions are separate conditions.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: The rule does not automatically prohibit flight solely because alcohol was consumed the previous evening; elapsed time, impairment, and alcohol concentration remain relevant.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The regulation specifies defined prohibitions rather than a universal zero-detectable-alcohol standard.

copyright_status: Original question wording based on United States federal regulation

subject: Navigation and Flight Planning
learning_objective: Select an appropriate VFR cruising altitude based on magnetic course and applicable rules.
question_text: An airplane is operating VFR in level cruising flight more than 3,000 feet above the surface on a magnetic course of 090 degrees. Which cruising altitude is appropriate under 14 CFR 91.159?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 4,500 feet MSL

choices.label: B
choices.text: 5,000 feet MSL

choices.label: C
choices.text: 5,500 feet MSL

choices.label: D
choices.text: 6,500 feet MSL

explanation: For a magnetic course from 0 degrees through 179 degrees, VFR cruising altitudes are odd thousands plus 500 feet. Therefore, 5,500 feet MSL is appropriate, subject to terrain, airspace, and other operational constraints.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 4,500 feet is an even-thousand-plus-500 altitude used for magnetic courses from 180 through 359 degrees.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: VFR cruising altitudes under this rule include the additional 500 feet.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: 6,500 feet is an even-thousand-plus-500 altitude used for westbound magnetic courses.

calculation_steps: Magnetic course 090° falls within 0°–179° → odd thousand + 500 feet → 5,500 feet MSL.

source_location: § 91.159 VFR cruising altitude or flight level

subject: Preflight Planning
learning_objective: Apply required preflight planning considerations to a proposed flight.
question_text: Before a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, which information must the pilot in command become familiar with under 14 CFR 91.103?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only the destination weather forecast

choices.label: B
choices.text: All available information concerning the flight, including fuel requirements, alternatives if the flight cannot be completed, known traffic delays, and runway lengths at airports of intended use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only aircraft performance data and passenger names

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only NOTAMs issued during the previous 24 hours

explanation: Section 91.103 requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight. For a flight not in the vicinity of an airport, specified items include weather reports and forecasts, fuel requirements, alternatives if the planned flight cannot be completed, known ATC traffic delays, runway lengths at airports of intended use, and takeoff and landing distance information.

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Weather is required but is only one part of the mandated preflight information.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Aircraft performance is relevant, but passenger names are not a substitute for the required information listed in the regulation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The obligation is not limited to NOTAMs or to a fixed 24-hour window.
